title: The Chaubole verses

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Funhe, landing again and again on har haan. Your line was rhythmic longing. When a missing came back, did it land as a refrain? Day one thousand two hundred seven.

What would you pay for love? It's an odd question until someone actually tries. A ring that costs too much. A trip meant to fix things. A gift that arrives instead of a person. On Ang thirteen hundred sixty-three, just past the Funhe, Guru Arjan's Chaubole take up that very question. They speak of love, and they name people as they go, calling out to listeners by name. And the first thing they say is about money, and what it can't do.
screen: `WHAT WOULD YOU PAY FOR LOVE?` → `ANG 1363.` → `WHAT MONEY CAN'T DO.`

segments.voice: The name is often heard as chau, four, and bole, things spoken: four sayings, or four voices. Readers explain the four in different ways, and the text itself doesn't stop to say. What's clear is the subject: love, prem, the love of the soul for the Lord. The verses call out to people by name, Samman and Musan among them, as if the Guru were turning to friends in a circle and speaking to each. Here's one, paraphrased. Samman, if this love could be bought with money, think of Ravan, the king of the old epic. He was no pauper, the verse says, and he gave his own heads, yet he could not buy it. That's the turn. A king with treasure to spare, willing to give even his own heads, still couldn't purchase it. Love of this kind isn't a sale. Other verses, paraphrased again, speak of love spread like moonlight across the sky, and of the bumblebee caught fast in the lotus it loves. Four voices, then, can mean something simple and human. Love gets talked about from more than one side. The one who longs, the one who's asked, the friend who watches, the Beloved who's silent. A single voice would make it a lecture. Several make it a conversation, and the conversation keeps coming back to the same discovery: what the soul wants most can't be bought, only given and received.
screen: `CHAU, FOUR; BOLE, SAYINGS.` · `CALLING OUT TO SAMMAN.` · `RAVAN COULDN'T BUY IT.` · `LOVE FROM MORE THAN ONE SIDE.` · then, large: `FOUR VOICES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one. If you can find the Chaubole on Ang thirteen hundred sixty-three, read one verse, and notice who it's speaking to. If you can't, sit with someone you love in mind, and let four voices take a turn: what you'd say to them, what they might say back, what a friend watching would say, and the quiet underneath. None of it needs to be spoken aloud. Then let the breath settle. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each out-breath. The bell holds the time.
The Chaubole verses. Guru Arjan's verses on love, often heard as four sayings, calling out to listeners by name. Today's word.
Your line: four voices. Today, before you speak in a disagreement with someone you love, let one other voice have a turn in your head: theirs. Day one thousand two hundred seven.

notes: The paraphrase of the first Chaubola (Samman, if this love could be bought with money; Ravan was no pauper, he gave his heads, yet could not buy it) is from memory; please check it against Ang 1363–1364.
The gloss of 'chaubole' as four sayings (chau, four; bole, spoken) and the note that readers explain the four in different ways should be confirmed by a Keeper.
The names Samman and Musan are given as addressees in the text; please confirm. Traditions about who they were are left out on purpose.

The summary of other verses (love spread like moonlight across the sky, the bee bound in the lotus, from the Musan verse 'maskar prem ki rahi ju ambar chhai; bidhe bandhe kamal meh bhavar rahe laptai') is from memory and should be checked.
